title: Railway Changelog #0309: Free VMs without an account
brief: Railway Changelog #0309 opens free Linux VMs with no account: `ssh railway.new` gets a 2 vCPU/2 GB box with coding agents preinstalled, 60 minutes to build and 24 hours to claim it before deletion. The same edition adds request tracing in Priority Boarding (edge-to-database waterfalls with no code changes) and OpenCode on Cloud Agents for persistent agent VMs.
details: Railway's changelog #0309 (September 25, 2026) with three launches. Free VMs without an account: `ssh railway.new` spins up a free Linux VM (2 vCPU, 2 GB RAM) with coding agents preinstalled and a preview URL — no signup or credit card; you get 60 minutes to build and 24 hours to claim the VM into an account before it is deleted. Tracing in Priority Boarding: follow a request from Railway's edge through your services into database calls as a timing waterfall, via OpenTelemetry SDK or automatic instrumentation, with agent skills updated so coding agents can use traces alongside logs and metrics. OpenCode on Cloud Agents: run OpenCode on a persistent Railway VM (`railway ca desktop --opencode` or `railway code --opencode`) and pick work up from anywhere; sleep keeps files on disk. Plus CLI fixes to `railway up` error output and installer reliability.

title: Orca
brief: A free, open-source Agent Development Environment (ADE): run Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Cursor CLI, and other CLI agents in parallel across isolated git worktrees, with a Ghostty-class terminal, in-app diff review, embedded browser, and SSH dev built in. Bring your own subscriptions — agents run side by side without interfering.
details: Orca is a free, open-source (MIT) Agent Development Environment — a desktop app for shipping with coding agents, positioned as a terminal-first Cursor alternative. It is worktree-first: each AI agent runs in its own isolated git worktree, so Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and 25+ other CLI agents (Grok, Gemini, Cursor, Copilot, Amp, Pi, Kiro, and more — bring your own subscription) can work side by side without conflicts. It bundles a Ghostty-class terminal with infinite splits, in-app diff review, an embedded browser, and remote SSH dev, with status tracking and notifications across parallel sessions. Recent releases added PDF diff preview, hidden-file quick-open, configurable worktree cards, and improved merge-conflict and CI review. Download for macOS, Windows, or Linux at onorca.dev.

title: heddlework
brief: A native, harness-neutral workspace for agent sessions: task graphs, diffs, and durable work across coding agents — Pi first, Codex and Claude next. Very early (~12 stars); expect rough edges.
warning: Very early (~12 stars); expect rough edges.
details: Heddlework is a native, harness-neutral workspace for agent sessions — built on the idea that the workspace (conversations, diffs, task graphs, review state) should outlive any one agent harness. Pi is the first adapter (rendered with GPUIX on macOS, Linux, and Windows), with Codex and Claude adapters planned; harnesses stay authoritative for execution while Heddlework projects their work into durable, searchable, GPU-rendered native surfaces including virtualized diffs, queued steering, session branches, and Fabric-powered orchestration. The status is honest: under active development and useful today as a source-built Pi desktop client, but not yet a signed or supported release. Install from source (`bun install`, `bun run setup:native`) or via the guided `install.sh`; a web/PWA companion and container host exist as previews. MIT, from monotykamary (Tom).

title: gpui-kit
brief: Rust GUI components for building cross-platform desktop apps on GPUI (the framework behind Zed). ~14.8k stars — one of the more-starred GPUI component libraries.
details: GPUI Kit is a comprehensive Rust desktop application framework built on GPUI (the UI framework from Zed Industries) — 75+ documented components and primitives with polished interactions, GPU-accelerated 120 FPS rendering, virtualized data tables and lists, a code editor stable at 200K lines with Tree-sitter and LSP, dock layouts, native Markdown/HTML rendering, AccessKit accessibility, UI integration testing, and WebAssembly support. Three layers: gpui-component (the complete styled system, best for applications), gpui-base (unstyled behavior and infrastructure, best for building your own design system), and gpui-shell (a JavaScript extension runtime). One dependency (`gpui-kit = "0.7"`) pins the matching GPUI release. It was extracted from Longbridge Pro, a publicly shipped commercial desktop app — production-proven rather than designed in isolation — and carries 15.8k stars. Apache-2.0 (docs prose CC BY 4.0); agent skills installable via `npx skills add longbridge/gpui-kit`.

title: scenario-labs/skills
brief: Agent skills for Scenario: image, video, audio, texture, 3D, and custom-model workflows over the Scenario MCP, aimed at games, entertainment, and creative verticals. Installs with `npx skills add scenario-labs/skills`; ~450 stars.
details: Agent Skills from Scenario that teach AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, and 70+ others) to produce production-ready images, video, audio, and 3D through the Scenario MCP server. The 65 skills cover the full creative pipeline — model picking, pricing before spending, character and brand consistency, storyboarding, product shots, textures, skyboxes, 3D assets, video editing, music, and custom model training — installable a la carte or grouped by role and goal via `npx skills add scenario-labs/skills`. A separate family of "expert tool" skills drives DCC software and game engines installed on your machine (Blender, Maya, ZBrush, Unreal Engine, Unity), distilled from expert tutorials, conference talks, and official docs. Requires the Scenario MCP server plus a Scenario account or API key. MIT, 850 stars.

title: Detail
brief: A curated gallery of the small UI decisions that make products feel considered — smarter word breaks, corner-morph animations, name-derived placeholders — each shown as a short clip. Curated by Rene Wang; a good reference for stealing micro-interaction ideas.
details: Detail (detail.design) is a curated gallery of the small interaction and copy decisions that make products feel considered — bite-size video examples like smarter word-break for translation-proof interfaces, hold-Option to reveal underlying details, name-derived placeholders, hold-to-reveal shortcut hints, inline regex testers, and adaptive text color. Curated by Rene Wang, it is more design-inspiration reference than component source: browse it when you want concrete, steal-able micro-interactions and UX copy patterns rather than generic UI kits. Also runs a social presence (@detaildotdesign) with exclusive content for followers.

title: Landbook
brief: A website design inspiration gallery with a large curated collection of landing pages, e-commerce sites, portfolios, and templates, plus boards for saving references. Useful for browsing real-world site design by category.
details: Land-book is a curated, daily-updated gallery of website design inspiration for creatives — hand-picked landing pages, portfolios, blogs, and ecommerce sites, browsable by category (landing, portfolio, blog, ecommerce), section, mobile, motion, OG images, and headlines, and sortable by most recent, recommended, most liked, or most viewed. Each entry shows the site with like counts and a copy link; some entries are paid Framer templates. A solid reference when you need real-world landing-page patterns rather than generic templates.

title: MaxiBestOf
brief: A website design and typography inspiration feed updated every weekday, pairing featured sites with their font stacks (e.g., Geist, Neue Haas Grotesk). A Pro tier adds private collections and HD screenshots.
details: MaxiBestOf (maxibestof.one) is a curated gallery of web design inspiration — websites, sections, and fonts — updated every weekday. Entries are organized by industry and type (agency, ecommerce, portfolio, fashion, technology, AI, restaurant, SaaS, editorial, and many more), and each featured site names the exact typefaces it uses (Space Grotesk, TWK Lausanne, Neue Haas Grotesk, Suisse Int'l, Geist Sans, ABC Diatype, GT Eesti, and dozens more) — useful when hunting for type-pairing ideas from real production sites. Also has a dedicated section-designs area with hero, footer, and newsletter section examples. A Pro tier adds private inspiration collections and HD screenshots, and there is a free weekly Monday newsletter of top sites.

title: SoulStack
brief: ProxySoul × Empryo: a bundle of skills, agents, an "immune system," and habits for coding agents. Very early (~17 stars); concept-heavy and expect rough edges.
warning: Very early (~17 stars); concept-heavy and expect rough edges.
details: SoulStack (proxysoul/SoulStack) is the published skill, preset, prompt, and habit collection behind Empryo — a coding agent from ProxySoul — packaged so you can point your own agent at it. Contents include skills like ensoul (reads the code and your vibe, builds a product's design system and redesigns its website, proven with screenshots), enliven (makes an app measurably faster with an A/B harness and an HTML report where every figure comes from JSON), marketing (turns product evidence into positioning without exposing private data), plus performance-traps, working habits, and takeaways rule sets. Its signature idea is an immune-system approach to testing: ten "immune cells" (tcell-hunter attacks, dendritic finds gaps, negative-selection kills false alarms, memory-cell turns confirmed bugs into permanent checks, natural-killer guards security, and more) grown per project. Installable per-skill via `npx skills add proxysoul/SoulStack`, as a Copilot plugin, or via a setup script that links skills and immune cells into Empryo, Claude Code, Copilot CLI, pi, OpenCode, and Gemini CLI — backing up every file it touches and adding a `soulstack` command for update/remove. Best in Empryo (live rule reload, genome-aware cells, background agents), with docs at soulstack.proxysoul.com.

title: GLiNER2.5-Decide
brief: Fastino's 340M-parameter open-weight model for schema-defined decision-making: feed it text plus typed questions and get valid answers with probabilities, confidence scores, and constraint-feasibility metadata. Apache 2.0, CPU-capable, strong on routing/triage/guardrail tasks. Benchmark figures are vendor-reported and not independently verified.
warning: Benchmark figures are vendor-reported and not independently verified.
details: Fastino's announcement of GLiNER2.5-Decide, a 340M-parameter open-weight (Apache 2.0) model built for schema-defined structured decision-making. Given text plus a set of typed questions — each with permitted answers, cardinality (single, multi, ordered), and cross-question rules — it returns answers with probabilities, confidence scores, and constraint-feasibility metadata. A constrained decoder evaluates related answers jointly, so decisions stay coherent (e.g., detecting prompt injection forces the safety verdict to `unsafe` rather than contradicting it). It also extracts character-level spans and relations and supports full or LoRA fine-tuning. Deliberately compact and non-generative: ~38ms p50 latency on a V100 GPU, ~167ms on a 48-vCPU CPU, runs locally and in air-gapped environments. Topped its unseen 17-dataset internal benchmark (60.1%) — intent routing, ticket triage, banking, sentiment, news topics — beating 4B-class decoder baselines. Natural fits: model routing, tool calling, browser/computer-use action selection, guardrails, context pruning, and LLM-as-judge.

title: kiro-fabric
brief: Kiro Fabric gives Kiro CLI a way to run several tool operations as one checked TypeScript program: Kiro writes the code, Fabric type-checks it and executes it in a fresh QuickJS context, with a repo-navigation layer (Navigator/Fovea) mapping symbols and change impact via ast-grep. warning: Fresh repo (0 stars, MIT); expect rough edges.
details: Kiro Fabric gives the Kiro CLI a "Code Mode": instead of many model/tool round trips, Kiro writes a small TypeScript program that runs several tool operations as one checked execution via the `@fabric/fabric_exec` tool — tools become async function calls supporting variables, conditions, loops, and bounded parallelism, executed in a fresh QuickJS context through a private MCP backend with type checking, argument validation, and approval policies. Its Fovea component ("Navigator", the `repo.*` API) maps repository structure with ast-grep into a symbol-and-relationship graph for focused code navigation, change-impact estimation, and hybrid search within a token budget. Requires macOS or glibc Linux, Node 24+, pnpm, ripgrep, and Kiro CLI 2.21.1+; install from the repo with `bash ./install.sh`. MIT, from asx8678. Note the documented limitation: as of September 2026, approval-dependent edits fail on newer Kiro CLI versions.

title: Claude Mods (function hooks proposal)
brief: Anthropic's design proposal for Claude Code "Mods" (function hooks): hook into Claude Code with TypeScript functions à la Express/Koa, with side-effect tracking and middleware-style composition — even modifying how components render. Committed to ship in weeks; the first three built-in mods' source listings are linked in the thread.
details: The GitHub issue where Anthropic proposed function hooks for Claude Code — TypeScript functions (Express/Koa-style, composed through a `$` sigil object) that let you hook deeply into Claude Code: modify behavior, restrict capabilities, even change how components render, with safety through side-effect tracking and a registration-order `next()` continuation model. Community feedback materially shaped the design; Anthropic committed to shipping within weeks under the product name "Claude Mods" (function hooks remain the engineering primitive), publishing the first three built-in mods' source and a public testing flag (`CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1`). The thread includes demo videos and a technical architecture doc. If you build Claude Code plugins, this is the thread tracking the extensibility primitive they will be built on.

title: Jev Decision Index
brief: A Hugging Face Space tracking benchmarks and news on the various repros of TypeSafe's Jev — a handy index if you're following the Jev model race.
details: A Hugging Face Space by multimodalart titled "Jev Decision Index", connected to the Jev retrieval tooling behind jevgrep (also in this library). The Space page is a JavaScript app whose content does not render for automated fetching, so this breakdown is thin: it appears to be an interactive demo or index around Jev's decision and relevance judgments. Worth opening directly if you use jevgrep and want to see the relevance engine's behavior firsthand.

title: jevgrep
brief: Find code by asking what it does: a CLI (plus an installable agent skill) that uses Jev to judge relevance across folders, files, and declarations, returning relevant files, reading leads, and verbatim source excerpts in one stdout response. Installs with `npm install -g @dzhng/jevgrep`; its own ten-task SWE-bench comparison claims ~30% lower coding-agent cost at equal task success. (~803 stars, MIT.) Cost figures are author-reported and not independently verified.
warning: Installs with `npm install -g @dzhng/jevgrep`; its own ten-task SWE-bench comparison claims ~30% lower coding-agent cost at equal task success. (~803 stars, MIT.) Cost figures are author-reported and not independently verified.
details: jevgrep is a CLI for coding agents that finds code by asking what it does: run `jg "How are telemetry events recorded and sent?" ./my-project` and it returns relevant files, reading leads, and verbatim source excerpts in one stdout response. It uses the Jev relevance engine to judge relevance across folders, files, and declarations (Python, TypeScript/JavaScript, Go, and Rust get declaration parsing), exploring the repo hierarchy rather than forcing results into a fixed top-k list. The pitch is cost: in their ten-task SWE-bench comparison it solved the same 8 of 10 tasks as the baseline at ~30% lower coding-agent cost. Requires Node 22+ and a key for Vercel AI Gateway, TypeSafe, OpenRouter, OpenCode Zen, or a TypeSafe-compatible endpoint; install the companion agent skill too (`jg skill`), since the CLI alone doesn't teach your agent to use it. MIT, from dzhng; searches send eligible source content to Jev, so choose a search root you intend to share.

title: rust-llm-tidy
brief: An opinionated linter aimed at LLM-generated code (Rust, C#, Markdown): fix/reorder/visibility/spacing transforms plus read-only lint checks, runnable per-file, on git-changed files, or in CI via a GitHub Action. The author's personal tooling ("largely written by LLMs"); expect opinionated rules, 0 stars. Apache 2.0.
details: An opinionated Rust (plus C# and Markdown) linter and tidier aimed squarely at LLM-written code, from Sewer56 — with the author's own preferences baked in and an upfront disclaimer that it is personal tooling, largely LLM-written and reviewed line by line, not held to production quality standards. One command (`rust-llm-tidy`) runs a pipeline of ops — GFM table alignment, fence-delimiter fixes, link hoisting, review-friendly item reordering, visibility narrowing, member spacing, plus read-only lints — with dry-run previews, JSON output, diff-base scoping, YAML config, and a GitHub Action to gate pull requests. Install via `cargo install rust-llm-tidy-cli` or prebuilt binaries from GitHub releases. Apache-2.0.

title: sys-prompt.md
brief: A complete agent-harness system prompt as a gist: JSON tool schemas for edit, glob, grep, question, read, shell, subagent, and write with execution semantics spelled out. Useful reference if you're building or tuning a coding-agent CLI.
details: A gist by Sewer56 publishing a `sys-prompt.md` — the system prompt and tool definitions for an agent harness, documenting its full tool surface as JSON schemas: edit, glob, grep, question (ask-the-user with choices), read (files, directories, images, PDFs), shell (zsh commands with timeouts and background execution), subagent (spawning child sessions, including codebase-explorer and web-search specialists), and write. Useful as a reference for what a well-specified agent tool API looks like — exact shapes, required fields, and behavioral notes (e.g., line-number prefixes are not part of file content; background commands notify on completion). If you are designing tool definitions for your own agent, this is a concrete template to crib from.

title: boxd
brief: Boxd offers "composable computers": persistent KVM dev VMs (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk by default) with live memory forking in under 200ms, snapshots, checkpoints, per-machine HTTPS subdomains, and a CLI/API plus MCP integrations for GitHub, Linear, and Slack — pitched for giving agents root and walking away. Billing is credit-based (about €0.22/h for a default machine per the site; €30 of free credits for new accounts). Pricing figures come from the site and are not independently verified.
warning: Pricing figures come from the site and are not independently verified.
details: boxd offers "composable computers" — persistent Linux VMs (real KVM virtual machines on Ubuntu 24.04, not containers) aimed at developers and AI agents, where running processes, open files, and shell state survive between sessions. The standout primitive is live memory forking: copy a running machine, disk and all, in under 200ms to experiment at the speed of thought, plus snapshots and in-place checkpoints (save points for memory and disk). The platform is fully configurable rather than a black box: checkpoints, snapshots, private domains, org-scoped secrets and env vars, GitHub/Linear/Slack integrations, an MCP server for Claude Code/Codex/opencode, per-machine HTTPS subdomains, and a self-hosted option. Billing is credit-based (about €0.22/hour for the default 2 vCPU/8 GiB machine while running; hibernated machines pay for disk only), every account starts with €30 free credits, and support is direct with the engineers — no ticket queue.

title: boat
brief: Boat sells cloud sandbox VMs for long-running agents: full VMs (Docker, systemd, databases), an integrated desktop/browser, and a CLI (`boat new`, `boat prompt` runs Claude Code or Codex inside), API, and SDKs, with stop/resume snapshots that pause billing. They claim $0.036/h for 4 vCPU / 8 GB RAM on a $20/mo plan ($20 of sandbox time), with a price table pitching themselves well under E2B, Daytona, Modal, and Vercel Sandbox. These price comparisons are the vendor's own and are not independently verified.
warning: These price comparisons are the vendor's own and are not independently verified.
details: boat.dev sells sandboxes for agents as full cloud VMs — real virtual machines where you can run Docker, systemd, databases, and cron, with an integrated desktop and browser for opening web apps, games, 3D scenes, and IDEs. You spawn up to thousands of sandboxes and drive them from the outside via CLI (`boat new/ssh/exec/prompt/events/host/desktop/stop/resume`), API, or SDKs: agents run inside while you prompt and observe from outside. Pricing starts at $20/mo converted into sandbox time, billed per second only while running (stopped sandboxes snapshot and pause billing), with 100–2,000 concurrent sandboxes by plan and EU regions (Germany, Finland, France). Their headline comparison claims a long-running agent workload costs $131/mo on boat versus $265–$1,764/mo across fourteen competitors — vendor numbers, treat as marketing until independently checked. The same team builds Battleships, the open agent-readable sandbox pricing comparison also in this library.

title: pi-better-skills
brief: A pi extension that fixes skill ergonomics: skills resolve their bundled files from the skill directory (`$PI_SKILL_DIR` instead of the workspace), each SKILL.md loads whole on first read, and path guidance is injected into the system prompt so authors stop babysitting paths. Installs with `pi install git:github.com/edxeth/pi-better-skills`; ~20 stars, POSIX-only.
details: A pi extension that fixes quality-of-life gaps in pi's Agent Skills support. The core problem it solves: pi runs tools from your workspace, so skills that bundle scripts, references, or templates break when they assume relative paths start at the skill folder — this extension makes skills resolve bundled files from the skill directory, injects a `<skill_context>` block so the model knows which paths belong to the skill versus the workspace, and ensures a SKILL.md loads whole on first read (no more rules lost to partial reads). It also adds skill composition via inline references, glob-based auto-injection, model and thinking overrides, and an option to convert pi's built-in docs prompt block into an on-demand skill to save context. Install with `pi install git:github.com/edxeth/pi-better-skills`; needs a POSIX environment (macOS/Linux, no Windows). From edxeth.

title: pi-coralbricks-provider
brief: An npm package (v1.0.19, by monotykamary — also behind pi-tool-repair and pi-mockdeck in this library) that registers CoralBricks as a provider extension for the pi coding agent: GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash through the Coral Inference API. It was shared in a support thread asking whether it uses completions or responses endpoints — check the repo README for the current endpoint behavior.
details: pi-coralbricks-provider is a provider extension for pi (the agentic coding framework) that routes model calls through the Coral Inference API, giving pi access to GLM 5.2/5.3, Kimi K3, and GPT-OSS 120B. Published on npm by monotykamary (Tom) under MIT, it plugs into pi's extension system so agent runs can use CoralBricks-served models as drop-in providers. The npm page itself blocks automated fetching, so this summary is drawn from the registry metadata and the package description rather than the rendered page. Useful if you run pi agents and want those models behind one inference endpoint.

title: The next Git platform on Cloudflare
brief: Cloudflare's blog announces a competition to build the next Git platform on Cloudflare, aimed at an AI-agent era of coding. Read it for the contest details and Cloudflare's take on where agent-driven development tooling is headed.
details: A Cloudflare blog post announcing a competition to build the next Git platform for the agentic era on Cloudflare Workers and Artifacts. The premise: GitHub was built for humans, but agents now write most code — so what should repositories, branches, pull requests, and code review look like when hundreds or thousands of agents work on the same codebase concurrently? It also announces new Artifacts capabilities in open beta: deploying Artifacts repos to Workers, managing repos from Workers via bindings, event subscriptions on repo activity, data jurisdiction controls, and dashboard metrics (billing starts October 15, 2026). To enter: submit a 5–10 minute demo video plus permissively licensed source by October 14, 2026; the top three teams fly to Cloudflare Connect in San Francisco and first place gets $25,000 in credits.

title: ccdeck
brief: ccdeck is a free, open-source local dashboard for Claude Code and Codex sessions — live session and tool-call views plus cost tracking. Useful if you run multiple agent sessions and want a single pane of glass.
details: ccdeck is a free, open-source (AGPL-3.0) live dashboard for Claude Code and OpenAI Codex CLI sessions that runs on your machine — start it with `npx ccdeck` or the desktop app (macOS, Windows, Linux). It draws every session, subagent, and tool call as a tree on one canvas, surfaces which session is waiting for your input (permission prompts, questions, and finished turns sorted longest-wait first, with desktop notifications), and tracks cost, token usage, and quota pace across Claude and Codex accounts — including multi-account switching and login sharing or repair across paired machines. It watches but cannot steer: the hook only forwards events, never approves tool calls or edits code. Privacy-conscious by design: sessions and prompts never leave the machine (the dashboard listens on 127.0.0.1); only version checks, quota reads with your own credentials, and opt-out usage reports go out.

title: hpc-sandbox-benchmarks
brief: A benchmark suite comparing sandbox providers using real high-performance developer and CI/CD workloads, shared as "new benchmarks in town". Check it when choosing between sandbox VM offerings for agents — the results are the author's own and are not independently verified.
warning: Check it when choosing between sandbox VM offerings for agents — the results are the author's own and are not independently verified.
details: hpc-sandbox-benchmarks compares sandbox providers on real high-performance developer and CI/CD workloads rather than synthetic micro-benchmarks. Every provider runs the same target hardware shape (4 vCPU, 8 GiB RAM, 40 GB disk) through end-to-end workflows developers actually experience — clone, dependency install, lint, build, test — because a provider can top a creation-time chart and still lose badly on thousands of small random file writes. Synthetics follow versioned Phoronix Test Suite profiles via OpenBenchmarking.org for reproducibility, and the methodology is strict: fresh sandboxes per result, pinned toolchains, raw samples retained, and failed or non-comparable results disclosed rather than zeroed. Results publish to a leaderboard with full dataset and architecture docs. MIT-licensed, from starslingdev.

title: Cua Spaces
brief: A free full-desktop Space for every agent — macOS VMs on machines you own or in your own cloud (Apple silicon Macs for macOS Spaces, Docker or Podman for Linux), connectable to Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Cline, Kiro and OpenClaw through the Cua MCP. Its Teleport feature moves an app's whole session (tabs, profile, sign-ins) from your Mac into a Space, with nothing read until you approve and Touch ID gating on sensitive items.
details: Cua Spaces gives every AI agent a free full desktop — a "Space" running as a VM or container on your Mac, machines you own, or your own cloud, streamed to you as a live desktop via Cua's RCDP remote desktop protocol (low latency over QUIC on local networks). Its Teleport feature moves an entire app session — open tabs, profile, sign-ins — from your Mac into a Space as an encrypted session bundle that nothing reads until you approve, with Touch ID gating on sensitive items and end-to-end sealing to the Space's own key. Spaces come agent-ready with permissions granted and tools installed; Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Cline, Kiro, and OpenClaw connect through the Cua MCP. Spaces on your own machines are free (hosted relay free during early access); the stack is source-available under FSL-1.1-MIT, converting to MIT two years after each release, with Cua Driver and Lume under MIT. Note: anonymous usage telemetry is on by default but can be switched off in settings. From the Cua team (trycua/cua on GitHub).

title: Battleships
brief: An agent-readable comparison of sandbox, VM and runtime pricing for AI agents — 366 providers priced through one engine with every figure quoted from the source pricing page, published as llms.txt, JSON files and a Node pricing engine. Built by boat.dev, one of the providers it ranks; the rankings are not independently verified, so take them with a grain of salt.
warning: Built by boat.dev, one of the providers it ranks; the rankings are not independently verified, so take them with a grain of salt.
details: Battleships is an agent-readable price comparison of sandbox, VM, and runtime providers for AI agents — 361 providers priced through one engine, with every figure quoted from the provider's own pricing page. Everything is published as plain files (llms.txt, per-provider JSON/Markdown with quoted evidence, and a Node pricing engine) so a coding agent can run the comparison for you. The methodology is strict: agents read pricing pages in a real browser, every answer links and quotes its source verbatim, unpublished prices are never read as free, and the same rules apply to boat.dev — the company that built it. What it can't check: whether features actually work end to end, reliability and uptime, sales and support quality, or company health. Data and code are open and contributions are welcome.

title: HostBrr
brief: European VPS and hosting provider (cloud VPS from €3.50/mo, web hosting from €1.25/mo) on AMD EPYC/Threadripper with NVMe storage, a 10Gbps network and included DDoS mitigation; Felix strongly recommends it for non-serious projects, citing best performance-per-dollar in Europe. Felix notes the site's "order" tab is quirky; the performance-per-dollar claim is the sharer's and is not independently verified.

details: A probability paper on Samuel Chen's blog proving that in the Hog dice game (from CS61A), rolling n dice maximizes the expected turn score for an n-sided die. It derives the expected turn score via the law of total expectation — accounting for the "Sow Sad" rule where any 1 collapses the turn score to 1 — then proves the maximum sits exactly at m = n by analyzing the sign of the marginal gain between rolling m+1 and m dice, with charts showing each curve peaking at m = n for 4-, 6-, and 10-sided dice. A neat, self-contained read if you like seeing a game-theory intuition made rigorous.

details: AgentFS (docs.turso.tech) — Turso's filesystem for AI agents. The core idea is copy-on-write isolation: run agents in sandboxed sessions where every file modification is isolated from your source tree, so the agent can mutate freely while the originals stay untouched. Everything lives in one portable SQLite database (easy to share and snapshot); every file operation is recorded and queryable for built-in auditing; optional sync of agent state to Turso Cloud. Ships two ways: a CLI that wraps an existing program in a sandboxed session, and an SDK for building custom agents on top of the filesystem abstraction. The natural answer to "what filesystem should my agent run on" for agent builders who want isolation, auditability, and portability without building a sandbox layer themselves.

brief: The live demo of the snowflow_demo repo below: real-time procedural snow rendering in the browser via WebGPU, Babylon.js, and hand-written WGSL — GPU-generated terrain, snow deformation, procedural characters, cloth, and post-processing with zero textures, meshes, HDRIs, or animation assets. Requires a WebGPU-capable browser (Chrome 113+ on desktop GPU) to load.

title: snowflow_demo
brief: Source repo for the Snowflow demo above: a fully procedural real-time snow scene built on WebGPU + Babylon.js with hand-written WGSL shaders — terrain, snow deformation, surf wakes, water spells, atmosphere, and post-processing, all generated at runtime. ~580 stars.

title: AoAgents
brief: An AI agent platform whose pitch is "Everything is an Agent". Announcement-level description only; details unverified since the link was not opened.
warning: Announcement-level description only; details unverified since the link was not opened.
details: AO (aoagents.dev) — an open-source agent orchestrator for running multiple coding agents in parallel. You describe the outcome; the main orchestrator plans the work and spawns workers into their own isolated git worktrees so they can work on different branches or features simultaneously without conflicts. Every session flows across one board (working / needs you / in review / ready to merge) with agent, branch, and PR state on the card. It watches every PR it opens and routes failed CI checks and review comments back to the session that owns the branch until approval. Supports ~25 CLI-based coding-agent harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Aider, Goose, more) with per-project agent choice, and a mobile companion app (paired over LAN or Tailscale) so you can watch sessions, open a terminal, and get notified when an agent needs you — while execution and code stay on your own machine. Runs as a local daemon; code never leaves localhost. Apache 2.0.

title: Phoenix (Arize AI)
brief: Arize AI's open-source observability platform for LLM apps — tracing, evaluation, and experimentation for agent and RAG workloads. A standard choice for watching what production agents actually do.
details: Arize Phoenix (Arize-ai/phoenix, ~11.7k stars) — the open-source AI observability platform for tracing, evaluation, datasets, and prompt experimentation. Core surface: OpenTelemetry-based LLM tracing, LLM-judge evaluation (response/retrieval evals), versioned datasets, experiment tracking across prompt/model/retrieval changes, a playground for comparing models and replaying traces, prompt management, plus PXI — a built-in AI engineering agent for debugging traces and iterating on prompts. Vendor- and language-agnostic: auto-instrumentation via OpenInference for LangGraph, LangChain, OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK, Vercel AI SDK, LlamaIndex, DSPy, CrewAI, and providers from OpenAI/Anthropic/Google to Bedrock, OpenRouter, LiteLLM. Get tracing in minutes: `pip install arize-phoenix && phoenix serve` (or `uvx arize-phoenix serve`), or `npx @arizeai/phoenix-cli setup` from your project dir to have your coding agent instrument the app. Deploy via Docker/Helm/Kubernetes; one-click buttons for Railway, Render, Google Cloud, Azure, AWS. Self-hosted and open source; Arize AX is the managed counterpart. Python and TypeScript sub-packages (otel, client, evals, MCP, CLI) for lightweight integrations.

title: Prime Agent (Prime Intellect)
brief: Prime Intellect's framework for training AI agents with reinforcement learning. Per the sharer, its gimmick is collecting training data through its CLI — worth a look if you're into RL-for-agents; specifics unverified.
warning: Per the sharer, its gimmick is collecting training data through its CLI — worth a look if you're into RL-for-agents; specifics unverified.
details: Prime Agent (PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent, ~21.5k stars) — an open-source coding and research agent built around two abstractions: a Recursive Language Model (RLM) that treats context as variables and recursive subagents as function calls inside a persistent Python REPL, and a Continual Harness that stores supplemental prompts, memories, skill descriptions, and reusable subagent specs as durable, refinable state. Key mechanics: everything is programmatic through the REPL (files, shell, tools, subagents); `rlm.spawn(...)` spawns real child agents for parallel/background work; `/refine` applies small evidence-backed updates to harness state (base system prompt is immutable, snapshots support rollback); skills are importable Python packages; daemon-backed agents keep running when the terminal disconnects; agents can communicate directly with each other; automatic compaction, persistent goals, heartbeats/schedules, and bounded autonomous mode (`/autonomous` with turn/token/time budgets) keep long tasks moving. Install: `curl -fsSL https://app.primeintellect.ai/prime-agent/install.sh | sh`. MIT licensed. Accompanies the arXiv paper "Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness".

title: windows-harness (browser-use)
brief: A Windows automation harness from the browser-use team (the web-agent library folks). Likely for running agents against Windows apps; details unverified.
warning: Likely for running agents against Windows apps; details unverified.
details: Windows Harness (browser-use/windows-harness) — "the simplest, thinnest harness that gives an LLM complete freedom to complete virtually any task on a PC." One persistent Python process connected directly to Windows, your real logged-in browser, and your files — no framework, no recipes, no rails; the agent writes what is missing mid-task in ordinary Python. Six primitives cover the whole desktop: `see` (screenshots even of background/occluded/minimized windows via PrintWindow), `key`, `type` (UIA set_value → foreground Unicode input → clipboard paste, escalating), `click`, `paste`, `ax` (raw UI Automation), `script` (PowerShell), plus `Path`/`subprocess` and a `browser` handle that lazily connects Browser Harness to your real Chrome. Honest about Windows input limits: foreground delivery is the default (holds foreground across bursts, hands back on `win.release()`), background is an opt-in that gets refused with a structured `BackgroundUnavailable` error when the target framework can't accept it. Every coordinate action stamps an action-proof screenshot (reticle/arrow/line) so the agent can verify where it landed. Install: `uv install` from PyPI, `windows-harness install-skill` to register with Codex/Claude Code/Cursor, then `windows-harness doctor`. Anonymous telemetry on by default (CLI category/success/duration only, no prompts or screenshots), can be disabled. Experimental, Windows 10 1809+/11, MIT.

title: Spec-PTC: Speculative Parallel Test-Time Compute
brief: A write-up of Spec-PTC, a speculative parallel test-time compute framework for long-horizon agents. Interesting if you follow inference-scaling tricks for agentic workloads.
details: Speculative Programmatic Tool Calling (alexzhang13.github.io) — a 2026 blog post by Alex L. Zhang (of RLM fame) proposing a latency trick for code-action agent harnesses: speculate and pre-launch tool calls from partially generated REPL calls while tokens are still streaming, rather than waiting for the whole generation to finish. The high-level design: imported tool calls get a hook so a "shadow REPL" (a deepcopy fork of the main code REPL, with unsafe functions like `open` marked as blocked) parses the partial output and launches speculatable calls asynchronously; when the real REPL later invokes them, they resolve from a promise store. Handles literals immediately, safely-computable dependencies after evaluation, and tracks unique instances of identical non-deterministic calls. Reported gains on RLMs: generally 1-1.2x on OOLONG benchmarks (Qwen3-30B-A3B, 8xH100 vLLM). The post surveys related work (Conveyor, Speculative Interaction Agents, AsyncFC) and links the full reference implementation (github.com/alexzhang13/spec-ptc). Worth reading for anyone building code-first agent harnesses.

title: Headlong (Laude Institute)
brief: An open-source agent microharness with persistent agency and recursive LLMs — "of bash, by bash". Minimal by design; good for experimenting with agent loops without a heavy framework.
details: Headlong (laude-institute/headlong, 1.2k stars) — an open-source agent microharness from the Laude Institute whose core is ~11K lines of Bash: "of bash, by bash, for bash; it's shells all the way down." Its defining idea is persistent agency — the agent never sleeps and keeps thinking in a self-guided loop between external interactions; messages from humans land in its thought stream as one more observation, and it decides whether and when to respond. One agent is built to be shared by a whole team over Slack, Telegram, and chat, all in a single timeline. At the heart is `shellm`, a Bash implementation of a recursive language model: the agent thinks by writing shell commands, running them, and reading the output. Tooling philosophy is pure Unix — small composable executables (`shellm`, `traj`, `llm`, `context`, `mem`, `skills`), trajectories as append-only jsonl DAGs with fork/merge, tiered context compaction at exponentially decaying resolution, subagents that see ancestors' trajectories, Docker by default, and self-improvement by fork-test-merge. One-line install (`curl https://headlong.ai/install.sh | bash`); alpha research software, run it sandboxed with a spend-capped key (~$1-2/hr thinking). Apache-2.0.

title: Shading Motion — Maxime Heckel
brief: Maxime Heckel's deep dive into shading-based motion design techniques. One of the better-written front-end animation articles; useful if you care about motion craft.
details: "Shading Motion" (blog.maximeheckel.com) — a deep, code-heavy creative-graphics essay by Maxime Heckel exploring motion as a creative medium: "how to shade motion." Using WebGPU compute shaders, he builds a pipeline that extracts motion via frame differencing (current vs previous frame luminance, thresholded and smoothed) and encodes it into motion masks and velocity maps, then treats those as inputs to effects: stylized trails with temporal decay, blob tracking by clustering motion regions, directional effects, optical flow, and motion blur with object smearing. The article is full of WGSL snippets (compute passes for the motion mask, render passes for heatmaps and pixelated trails) and interactive widgets demonstrating each stage on 3D scenes, videos, and webcam input. Compounds elegantly with his earlier post-processing work (volumetric lighting, atmospheric scattering, pixel manipulation). A strong reference for anyone doing WebGPU/R3F post-processing who wants to treat motion — not luminance or depth — as the primary shading input.

title: Radius — The AI Browser for Research
brief: An AI-native browser aimed at research workflows. Product claims unverified; notable as another entry in the agentic-browser wave.
warning: Product claims unverified; notable as another entry in the agentic-browser wave.
details: Radius (radiusbrowser.com) — a Chromium-based macOS browser that doubles as an IDE for running coding agents in parallel next to your PRs, docs, terminals, and localhost servers. The core idea: everything is a tab — your agent runs in a tab, so does the terminal, the diff viewer, and every PR, doc, dashboard, and localhost server you keep open, so context never gets lost switching windows. Spaces auto-organize per project; git worktrees get their own tab groups. Privacy posture is local-first: worktrees, sessions, and agent state live on your machine; agents authenticate with their providers directly (Claude, Codex, or Cursor — use the subscription you already have); analytics can be opted out of at any time. Free; Radius adds no additional subscription beyond your existing agent accounts. Download for Apple Silicon or Intel.

title: darkbloom — MCP gateway
brief: An MCP (Model Context Protocol) gateway that advertises an accuracy guarantee — unusual positioning in the MCP tooling space. Claims unverified; interesting if you run MCP servers in production.
warning: Claims unverified; interesting if you run MCP servers in production.
details: Darkbloom (darkbloom.dev, by Eigen Labs) — "the only MCP gateway with an accuracy guarantee," an unusual positioning in the MCP tooling space that makes it worth a look if you run MCP servers in production. The underlying network is a decentralized compute grid of hardware-attested Apple Silicon Macs (the homepage quotes ~1,231 Macs, 287B tokens generated, 72M requests): each request is end-to-end encrypted on your device, decrypted only inside a hardened process on an attested node, and the response is signed by the specific machine that produced it, so the node operator can never see your prompts. The API is OpenAI-compatible (api.darkbloom.dev/v1, cursor SDK examples exist); community integrations include Shroud TEE proxy routing. First response per session can be slow (15-60s warm-up) per community notes; product claims beyond the public docs are unverified.

title: pi harness v2 docs (earendil-works)
brief: Deep link into the pi coding agent's v2 harness documentation. Worth reading if you use pi or are designing your own agent harness.
details: Pi harness-v2 design doc (earendil-works/pi, branch harness-v2/j4) — a 3,446-line Durable AgentHarness design document for the pi coding agent, worth reading if you use pi or are designing your own agent harness. Core concepts: durable runs (an accepted prompt is a durable operation — after a crash a new process restores the session and resumes from the last safe boundary, with no partial outcomes); lanes (a session hosts one or more named positions in the conversation tree, each running at most one operation at a time, executing in parallel — e.g. a Slack thread per lane); a session = append-only conversation tree + lanes + per-lane operation logs + global facts; single writer per session; deterministic stepping where every effect crosses an injectable boundary (a `manual` drive mode parks before each effect so tests can drive crash-recovery call by call); hooks that intercept execution vs events that only observe; tiered context compaction. Backward-compat requirement is only that old coding-agent v3 JSONL sessions open and restore idle. A serious piece of harness engineering, not a README.

title: ThreeUI
brief: A browsable library of Three.js components and interactive shaders. Handy for dropping 3D effects into web projects without writing raw WebGL.
details: ThreeUI (threeui.com/browse) — a browsable library of Three.js components, templates, and interactive shaders for dropping 3D effects into web projects without writing raw WebGL. The catalog is organized by section type (Testimonials, Footers, Pricing, Features & Benefits, How It Works, Call to Action, About & Story, Product Showcases…) with each entry extracted from a complete authored page — e.g. glass testimonial cards with iridescent helixes, shader-lit pricing calculators, 3D cylinder client carousels, animated parchment footers — preserving assets, motion, and responsive layout. Handy reference library for front-end devs who want production-quality 3D flourishes as copyable components rather than starting from shaders.

title: kolu
brief: A terminal tool that bills itself as "the best way to run terminals". Details unverified, but worth a look if your terminal setup needs rethinking.
warning: Details unverified, but worth a look if your terminal setup needs rethinking.
details: kolu (kolu.dev) — a terminal tool that bills itself as "the best way to run terminals," aimed squarely at the agent era. The pitch: keep the Mac as the window, run agents on Linux — a headless box is fast (especially the filesystem) and stays up; your Mac gets a real launcher app showing real terminals on an infinite canvas running claude, codex, opencode, grok, pi, xyne, omp, or anything in a shell. The dock mirrors every terminal (repo, agent, how long it's been waiting); a pinned "Needs-you" strip surfaces permission questions from any agent no matter how buried its tile is; answer inline (maximize tile, approve) without tab-hunting. A built-in code browser lets you leave PR-style review comments on lines and hand them to the agent in one paste. Another machine is one tab away via SSH (only Nix needed on the far end). Free and open source (AGPL-3.0), self-hosted, no account. The team blogs about their Effect 4-based architecture.

title: anti-slop (dmmulroy)
brief: Opinionated Oxlint rules that reject low-evidence TypeScript/JavaScript patterns — basically a linter config against AI-slop code. Fun and practical for teams drowning in generated code.
details: anti-slop (dmmulroy/anti-slop, ~5.1k stars) — opinionated Oxlint rules that reject low-evidence, low-signal TypeScript/JavaScript patterns — "a linter config against AI-slop code." Roughly 20 generic rules (no-array-filter-map, no-chained-type-assertions, no-unknown-returns/params, no-widen-then-assert, no-runtime-typeof, no-module-mocking, require-safety-comment-for-type-assertion…) plus an opt-in Effect rule group (no-manual-effect-error-tag, prefer-effect-match…). The project is explicitly meant to be vendored, not npm-installed: a bundled agent skill (`npx skills add dmmulroy/anti-slop --skill install-anti-slop`) copies the plugin into your repo, merges it into your lint config, matches your existing Oxlint version, and three-way-merges updates while preserving local customizations. Rules use Oxlint's ESTree/scope APIs rather than a full type checker, and the README documents each violation with before/after examples. MIT.

title: Introducing Slack Code (Salesforce)
brief: Salesforce's announcement of Slack Code, bringing coding-agent workflows into Slack. Announcement-level; the "oh no" from the sharer suggests healthy skepticism.
details: Slack Code (salesforce.com announcement) — Salesforce's "agentic coding is now multiplayer" product: dedicated code channels in Slack where teams and coding agents write, review, and ship code together in the open. Tag in a coding agent and it spins up a code channel; everyone in the channel sees the conversation, reviews diffs, checks live previews, gives feedback, and approves before anything ships; the channel archives itself when done while history stays searchable. Launch partners building agents for it: Anthropic (Claude), Cognition (Devin), GitHub (Copilot), ChatGPT, Vercel. Beyond code channels, the announcement adds an Agents tab (browse all agents/sessions, statuses, stop mid-task), Agent DMs with real thread titles, and Add to Slack one-click agent publishing from NanoClaw, Lovable, n8n, LangChain, etc. Security posture: agents inherit Slack's permissions and admin controls, and high-stakes moves like pushing to production require an in-channel human sign-off. Available on any Slack plan (partner agent access required); pricing/packaging subject to change.

title: claudish-to-english (gvzdv)
brief: A small repo that translates "Claudish" — AI-assistant jargon — into plain English. Niche but amusing; useful if you've ever stared at a model hedging for three paragraphs.
details: claudish-to-english (gvzdv, ~2.7k stars) — a Claude Code plugin that shows a plain-English rewrite of each assistant message, produced by a local LLM via ollama (default, e.g. gemma4:26b-mlx), the Codex CLI, the Anthropic API, or any OpenAI-compatible API. It is strictly display-only: Claude's reasoning and the saved transcript keep the original text; only what you read on screen changes. Controlled live via `/claudish` (on/off, append/replace display modes, styles like tldr/5y/caveman, output language, model — changes take effect mid-session and persist via flag files), plus `CLAUDISH_*` env vars for durable defaults. An optional second hook rewrites Markdown files into plain language on write (opt-in, off by default). Every hook fails open — provider down, timeout, or missing model and you just see the original text with a one-time notice, never a swallowed or corrupted answer. Privacy note: with the default ollama provider everything stays local. MIT.

title: interior.dev
brief: Micro-interactions for React, "built for the half-second after a click". A focused little library for the small animations that make UIs feel alive.
details: interior.dev — free, open-source React micro-interaction components, "argued out to the frame": buttons, spinners, copy buttons, and the fiddly half-second-after-a-click details that make software feel expensive instead of cheap. The model is shadcn-style — one file per component, you keep the source and restyle freely (React + Tailwind + Motion, TypeScript throughout). Install via `npx shadcn@latest add https://www.interior.dev/r/copy-button.json`. The behavior is finished; the style is yours. MIT licensed. Named "Library of the Month" on 21st.dev.

title: eve — durable AI agent framework
brief: A durable agent framework pitched as "Next.js for agents" — build agents with one folder, with durability baked in. Product claims unverified; the durability angle is the interesting bit.
warning: Product claims unverified; the durability angle is the interesting bit.
details: eve (eve.dev) — a filesystem-first, Apache-2.0 framework for building durable backend AI agents, pitched as "like Next.js for agents" — "build durable agents with one folder." You add channels, tools, skills, sandboxes, hooks, and schedules through filesystem conventions and deploy agent workloads on Vercel or self-host them as Node services. The site is agent-friendly by design: docs and integration pages expose Markdown via `.md`/`.mdx` extensions, with `/llms.txt`, `/llms-full.txt`, and a semantic sitemap for agent navigation. A template gallery bootstraps common shapes: persisted chat with per-user long-term memory, an LLM council (four models + judge), Slack agents, a GitHub maintainer (weekly digests, PR summaries, @mentions, Linear delegation), a software factory (classifier → analyst → implementer → reviewer → draft PR), incident response with live Datadog/GitHub/Vercel evidence, and marketing/social/Sanity/Mux agents. Currently in beta.

title: OpenHistory
brief: Turns your Mac activity into a private timeline for you and your AI — local activity history as agent context. Privacy-sensitive by nature; the "private" claim is unverified.
warning: Privacy-sensitive by nature; the "private" claim is unverified.
details: OpenHistory (openhistory.sh) — an open-source, local-first Mac app that turns your activity into "a private timeline for you & your AI." It observes foreground apps and the macOS Accessibility context you permit (window names, document context, browser domains, visible interface text) — no screenshots, audio, camera, keystrokes, passwords, or private browsing — and summarizes the day into a timeline of completed work, decisions, and unfinished work. Privacy posture is explicit: everything stored in a permission-restricted local directory, no analytics/telemetry, on-device summaries via Apple on-device models or fully off; cloud providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Kimi) are opt-in with your own key and an approved disclosure. Approved local agents (ChatGPT Desktop, Claude Cowork, any local-MCP agent) get a redacted, read-only view through an authenticated MCP server running only on your Mac. Pause at any time, exclude apps, and "delete all local data" wipes everything. Requires macOS 14+.

warning: Product claims unverified.

title: fx — Vercel Labs coding agent
brief: Vercel's announcement of fx, "a tiny, open, native coding agent" from Vercel Labs, originally an internal tool. Announcement-only source; details unverified.
warning: Announcement-only source; details unverified.
details: fx (Vercel Labs) — announced via the Vercel Developers X account as "a tiny, open, native coding agent," originally an internal tool. It is a Unix-like coding-agent CLI written in Zig (vercel-labs/fx, Apache-2.0, ~3.3k stars): a single ~6-8 MiB native binary with no hosted service and no public HTTP API — just the binary. It runs in four places: the terminal (with a shell-like scrollback UI rather than a full-screen TUI), shell scripts, ACP-speaking editors, and your own Node app via `libfx` (the same agent core embedded in your product, with tools written in JavaScript). Model-agnostic: sign in with Vercel AI Gateway, reuse a ChatGPT or Grok subscription, or point it at a local Ollama server. Security-minded: a cloned project's files can't choose your model or permission rules, and bundled MCP servers don't start until you trust them. Marked experimental (0.0.x at announcement); community deep dives and an fx-on-workers demo (libfx WASM in a Cloudflare Worker) already exist. (The link is the X announcement; the project detail above is corroborated from the public repo and independent coverage.)

title: skills (emilkowalski)
brief: A collection of "skills" for designers and engineers from Emil Kowalski (of Vercel/animations fame). Likely agent-skill style playbooks; worth browsing.
details: emilkowalski/skills (~43k stars) — "Skills for Designers and Engineers" from Emil Kowalski (Vercel/Linear, animation fame), a set of agent skills for building better interfaces. The premise: "agents don't have great taste" — they pick ease-in for enter animations when it should be ease-out, solid borders where a semi-transparent shadow belongs — and these skills list the little mistakes agents make and how to fix them, a shortcut to standing out "in a sea of slop." Skills include: emil-design-eng (the main one, mostly animation plus design advice), animate (build an animation from scratch with correct curves/durations/properties), animate-expo (React Native gestures/sheets/haptics, off the JS thread), review-animations (strict audit by his rules), improve-animations (prioritized self-contained plans any agent can execute), find-animation-opportunities, animation-vocabulary, apple-design (WWDC principles translated for the web), write-swift, pick-ui-library, prototype, mobile-native, break-ui (worst-case data testing), and ask-sonner (his toast library). Install: `npx skills@latest add emilkowalski/skills`. MIT.

title: GPS-01 — interactive GPS explainer
brief: A tiny interactive explainer of how your phone finds itself — satellites, signal timing, and trilateration. The good kind of technical storytelling.
details: GPS-01 (gps-01.dmytro.fyi, by Dmytro Kondakov) — a tiny, playful interactive explainer of how your phone finds itself: satellites orbiting 20,200 km above Earth broadcasting nanosecond-accurate timestamps at light speed. The interface is the whole demo — click or tap anywhere on the globe to place a receiver ("that's you, holding a phone") and watch the telemetry panel (position, sim offset, tracking, FIX/3, FIX/4, CLOCK/4, geometry) work through trilateration live. The good kind of technical storytelling: one screen, one idea, satellites plus signal timing plus a bit of math. Report issues to the author via DM.

title: Rare UI

details: Rare UI (rareui.com) — a free, open-source collection of "rare" animated React components: 21+ unique components (orb effects, tactile sidebars, portfolio flourishes) aimed at making products stand out rather than blending into shadcn sameness. One file per component, installed with the shadcn CLI under any package manager. The homepage is mostly social proof — dozens of designers and engineers report shipping Rare UI components in real products and portfolios, with comparisons to Skiper UI — but the components themselves are browsable in action on the site. Solid option in the crowded React-animation-component space; compare with the other UI libraries already in the archive.

title: Cua Computer History (open source)
brief: Cua's announcement of the first open-source "Computer History", in early preview. Announcement-only; interesting for computer-use agent research.
details: Cua Computer History (announced via @trycua on X) — "the first open-source Computer History," in early preview for Cua Driver. It gives users an encrypted, device-local record of what Cua Driver did: which actions ran, which applications were targeted, which actions were confirmed/partial/refused/unverifiable, when history was enabled/paused/resumed/deleted. The privacy boundary is the headline feature and is permanent: no screenshots, no raw keystrokes or typed text, no clipboard contents, no raw tool arguments/results, no accessibility trees, no file paths, no free-form diagnostics. Preview 0 is action-history-first — it records only Cua-mediated session lifecycle events after you opt in (`cua-driver history enable`), never ambient desktop activity; 7-day retention, 100 MiB encrypted-store quota. Agents get two permission-gated read-only tools (`history_status`, `history_query`), with an access-audit event recorded; they cannot enable, pause, delete, export, or obtain the key. Docs live in trycua/cua under libs/cua-driver/docs/ (architecture, preview guide, agent-integration RFC). (x.com is not directly fetchable from this environment; the product detail is corroborated from the public repo docs.)

title: watermarks-remover (guillaumemeyer)
brief: Strips multi-vendor AI provenance marks — Unicode text hygiene, statistical rewrite hooks, and C2PA handling. Legitimate hygiene tooling; obviously dual-use.
details: watermarks-remover (guillaumemeyer, ~23.3k stars) — a privacy-first app plus agent skill and stdlib-Python service that strips multi-vendor AI provenance marks from content you own. Three layers: A (deterministic scripts for invisible Unicode, exotic spaces, bidi, tag chars), B (statistical token-sampling text watermarks via agent rewrite), and file metadata (C2PA/EXIF/XMP/doc properties across PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, HEIC, PDF, DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, EPUB, MP4/MOV, WAV/MP3/FLAC…). Coverage spans Claude, Gemini/SynthID-Text, OpenAI provenance surfaces, and open-LLM Kirchenbauer-style and keyed-Gumbel marks. Distributed three ways: a Claude Code plugin/marketplace (two slash skills), an install script for Claude Code/Cursor/Cowork (the skill is markdown-only and drives the service over HTTP, so the agent host needs no Python), and a stdlib-only HTTP service with `/detect`, `/watermark`, and `/clean` endpoints plus Docker compose. A `PostToolUse` hook can deterministically clean files the agent writes (check or clean mode). Includes benchmarks, verification harnesses, a pre-commit hook, and an honest ethics/disclaimer section about what removal costs and residual risk. MIT.

title: codedb (justrach)
brief: A Zig code-intelligence server and MCP toolset for AI agents, recommended firsthand by the sharer. Native-speed code intelligence as agent context is a strong pitch.
details: codedb (justrach, ~1.4k stars) — a Zig code-intelligence server and MCP toolset for AI agents: "big repo, little map." It draws the map your agent needs: file trees with symbol counts, outlines, symbol definitions and callers, call paths A→B, trigram-accelerated search, dependency graphs, portable snapshots, and remote GitHub repo queries via a DeepWiki-style remote MCP. Seventeen MCP tools by default (`codedb_context`, `codedb_explain`, `codedb_callpath`, `codedb_search`, `codedb_deps`…); a context engine, not an editor — it has no edit tool, you use your client's native editing. Installers auto-register it in Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Windsurf, Devin, Copilot CLI, OpenCode and more; npm ships as `codedeebee` (name squat) with SHA256-verified native binaries. Parsers for Zig, C/C++, Python, TS/JS, Rust, Go, PHP, Ruby, HCL, R, Dart, OCaml. Structural search runs locally; the default hybrid retrieval uses hosted embeddings, with `semantic=local` for on-device-only. Alpha; BSD-3-Clause. There's also a companion desktop app (Harness) from the same org.

title: codebase-memory-mcp (DeusData)
brief: Persistent semantic memory for coding agents — an MCP server that indexes your codebase. Useful when you have many repos and context windows aren't enough.
details: codebase-memory-mcp (DeusData, ~45.7k stars) — a high-performance, pure-C code-intelligence MCP server that indexes codebases into a persistent knowledge graph: claims average repos in milliseconds, the Linux kernel (28M LOC, 75k files) in 3 minutes, sub-ms structural queries, and up to 120x fewer tokens than file-by-file exploration (83% answer quality, 10x fewer tokens, 2.1x fewer tool calls across 31 real repos in the associated arXiv preprint 2603.27277). Tree-sitter AST analysis across 162 vendored languages, enhanced with Hybrid LSP semantic resolution for 12 major languages; 17 MCP tools (search, trace, architecture, impact analysis, dead-code detection, Cypher queries, ADR management); a built-in 3D graph visualization UI served from the binary; infrastructure-as-code indexing (Dockerfiles, K8s manifests as graph nodes); single static binary, zero dependencies, no API key, 45 supported client surfaces. Security posture is explicit: full source open, per-release VirusTotal scans, SHA-256-pinned artifacts, 100% local processing, SECURITY.md with a known Defender false-positive disclosure. MIT.

title: quickbeam (elixir-volt)
brief: A JavaScript runtime for the BEAM — Web APIs backed by OTP, native DOM, and a built-in TypeScript toolchain. Genuinely novel: Erlang's concurrency model meets JS.
details: QuickBEAM (elixir-volt/quickbeam) — a JavaScript runtime for the BEAM: Web APIs backed by OTP, a native DOM, and a built-in TypeScript toolchain. The core idea: JS runtimes are GenServers — they live in supervision trees (crash recovery included), send and receive messages, and call into Erlang/OTP libraries, all without leaving the BEAM. JS can call Elixir handlers via `Beam.call`, send to any PID, monitor processes, and even do `Beam.rpc` across connected nodes; contexts can be pooled for high-concurrency workloads (e.g. one pool behind a Phoenix LiveView mount, each context with its own global scope, memory limits, and opcode budgets). An isolated `QuickBEAM.VM` mode decodes QuickJS bytecode with a BEAM interpreter for bounded evaluation with per-call fresh heaps — good for SSR-style workloads with step/memory/timeout limits. Supports browser APIs, Node.js compatibility, granular API groups (fetch, websocket, crypto, dom… down to 58 KB for bare), TypeScript compile support, npm packages, and bytecode disassembly for introspection. Install as a hex package (`{:quickbeam, "~> 0.11.2"}`); precompiled NIFs via Zig. MIT.

title: Qwen3.6-27B-MTP-GGUF (unsloth quant)
brief: Unsloth's GGUF quantization of Qwen3.6-27B with MTP (multi-token prediction). For local inference of the 27B Qwen.
details: Qwen3.6-27B-MTP-GGUF (unsloth) — GGUF quantizations of Qwen3.6-27B with Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) enabled, for ~1.5-2x faster local inference with no accuracy loss. Qwen3.6-27B is the first open-weight Qwen3.6: a 27B causal LM with a vision encoder, built for agentic coding — 64 layers of a Gated DeltaNet + Gated Attention hybrid layout, 262K native context (extensible to ~1M), thinking preservation, and improved tool calling. Unsloth's MTP build runs in llama.cpp (`--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2`), also loadable in Unsloth Studio (which auto-tunes MTP per hardware) with Dynamic 2.0 quants and developer-role support for Codex/OpenCode. Serving recipes for SGLang, vLLM (qwen3_next_mtp speculative config), KTransformers, and Transformers are documented. Good for anyone self-hosting Qwen3.6 and wanting draft-speculative speedups without changing outputs. License follows the upstream Qwen release.

Qwen3.8-27B highlights: 262K native context (YaRN-extensible to 1M), thinking mode on by default with per-request disable and `reasoning_effort` control, stronger autonomous planning and environment feedback for long-horizon agentic work; Alibaba claims 61.7 on SWE-bench Pro and Terminal Bench 2.1 gains over Qwen3.6 (maker-reported, independent validation pending). The ecosystem picked it up fast: Unsloth GGUFs, Ollama builds, OpenRouter routes, and top-5 most-liked on Hugging Face within two days.
