title: Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (unsloth quant)
brief: Unsloth's GGUF quantization of Qwen3.8-27B for local inference. The practical artifact behind the open-weights announcement above.
details: Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (unsloth) — Unsloth's Dynamic 3.0 GGUF quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B (1-bit through 16-bit), which Unsloth claims delivers >10% better top-1 accuracy at the same size than other providers. Qwen3.8-27B is "the most capable generation in the Qwen open-model family to date": a 27B dense model on the Qwen3.5 architectural foundation (16 × [3 × (Gated DeltaNet → FFN) + 1 × (Gated Attention → FFN)]), a native vision-language model understanding images, videos (hour-scale), STEM diagrams, and documents, with 262K native context (up to 1M). Thinking is on by default, disable-able per request, with tunable `reasoning_effort` and `preserve_thinking` for multi-turn agent work; Apache 2.0, commercial use allowed. Runs in Unsloth Desktop with thinking toggles, with recommended sampling params documented (temp 1.0/top_p 0.95 thinking, temp 0.7/top_p 0.80 instruct). ~6.3M downloads last month at card time; 1,305 derivative quants on the tree. The compact deployment-friendly counterpart to the 2.4T-A95B flagship — the one most teams will actually run on a single GPU.

title: pi-acp-jetbrain (ryan-brosas)
brief: A JetBrains IntelliJ ACP (Agent Client Protocol) adapter for the pi coding agent. Niche but exactly what you need if you want pi inside IntelliJ.
details: pi-acp-jetbrain (ryan-brosas) — an Agent Client Protocol (ACP) adapter that runs the pi coding agent inside JetBrains IntelliJ (IntelliJ is the primary host; other ACP clients get partial coverage). Architecture: the adapter is an ACP server over stdio; each session spawns one `pi --mode rpc` subprocess and translates messages — assistant text streams as `agent_message_chunk`, reasoning as `agent_thought_chunk`, tool runs as `tool_call`/`tool_call_update`, slash commands and pi skills surface as ACP commands (`/skill:<name>`). The JetBrains bridge is the standout: IntelliJ's built-in MCP server descriptor is exposed to pi as `ide_<server>_<tool>` extension tools, guarded by two allowlists, with three coding modes (`off`/`prefer`/`required`) where mutations can flow through IntelliJ's own apply_patch/rename/reformat — plus a per-turn inspection gate that flags files changed without an IDE mutation event. Install: `pi install npm:pi-acp-jetbrain` (or `npm install -g pi-acp-jetbrain`), register in `~/.jetbrains/acp.json`; npm releases carry signed provenance. MIT.

title: Woxi (vs Mathematica comparison)
brief: Woxi's comparison of itself against Mathematica — Woxi being an interpreter for a subset of the Wolfram Language. A decent way into what Woxi is and where it stands.
details: Woxi vs Mathematica (woxi.ad-si.com docs) — the comparison page for Woxi, an alternative to WolframScript, and Woxi Studio, an alternative to the Mathematica notebook frontend. Woxi aims for compatibility with the Wolfram Language but deliberately deviates in a few UX ways: Unicode identifiers (`woxi eval 'N[2π * 4]'`), direct evaluation of `.nb` notebook Input/Code cells from the command line (`woxi run notebook.nb` — something WolframScript can't do), and even an `Import` for CERN ROOT files (1-D/2-D histograms, TTree branch data, TLorentzVector) that the Wolfram Language doesn't natively support. Woxi Studio runs cells strictly top-down (no out-of-order evaluation) and drops `%` (last-result reference) as too brittle for kernel-state clarity. Honest coverage of what's missing: the Wolfram Knowledgebase, ML/neural nets, optimization, FEM, chemistry, audio/video computation, and per-release marquee features are mostly unimplemented, with conformance gaps against `wolframscript` catalogued and verified but not yet fixed. Worth reading if you do symbolic computation on a CLI budget.

title: spec-kit (GitHub)
brief: GitHub's official toolkit for spec-driven development — write the spec, let agents implement. From GitHub itself, so it carries weight in the SDD workflow trend.
details: Spec Kit (github/spec-kit, ~140k stars) — GitHub's open-source toolkit for giving AI coding agents structured processes, reusable templates, and documented outcomes. Three independent entry points: Spec-Driven Development (define what/why before how — `/speckit-constitution` once per project, then `/speckit-specify` → `/speckit-plan` → `/speckit-tasks` → `/speckit-implement` → `/speckit-converge` per feature, repeating implement→converge until it reports Converged), bug fixing (assess → fix → test, with a recorded verdict of verified/partial/failed — "missing verification is not a successful fix"), and idea assessment (intake → research → define → shape → decide, ending in go / needs-clarification / kill). The commands are agent skills invoked in your agent's chat, not terminal commands; extensions add capabilities, presets adapt behavior, workflows automate steps, bundles package role-based setups. Setup: `uv tool install specify-cli`, then `specify init my-project --integration copilot` (supports many agents; English/Chinese/Japanese READMEs). MIT.

title: pullfrog
brief: An open-source, model-agnostic, BYOK GitHub bot that runs in GitHub Actions. Bring your own key, pick your model, automate your repo — the self-hosted answer to proprietary coding agents.
details: Pullfrog (pullfrog/pullfrog, ~1.3k stars) — "the BYOK CodeRabbit that runs in your GitHub Actions." It's not an agent itself; it wraps vanilla Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode (whichever matches your BYOK or subscription configuration) and listens for GitHub events — PRs opened, issues created, reviews submitted, CI failures — triggering agent runs from a `pullfrog.yml` workflow via the open-source action. You control the infrastructure, the keys, and the costs. Out of the box: auto-review on new PRs (verdicts can gate merges via status checks), addressing review comments, CI autofix, merge-conflict autofix, issue triage, and `@pullfrog` ad-hoc invocation. Batteries included: a purpose-built MCP server for git/GitHub ops, isolated shell without sensitive env, a headless browser for e2e/screenshots, short-lived auto-revoked installation tokens, hooks (setup/post-checkout/pre-push/stop — a failing stop script resumes the agent with context), and GitHub-native permissions. Pricing: free for personal accounts and open source; Pro is $30/mo per org, no per-run or per-seat. The same action works standalone as a pipeline step with a JSON-schema `output_schema` for structured output. MIT.

title: DeepSeek Harness (developer preview)
brief: DeepSeek's agent harness in developer preview — "everything is a plugin", with source released alongside. Every agent capability is a swappable plugin; the plugin architecture is the interesting idea here. Claims unverified.
warning: Claims unverified.
details: DeepSeek Harness (deepseek.com/harness, `dsh`) — DeepSeek's open-source (MIT) agent harness, launched in developer preview. The architecture's headline: "everything is a plugin" — models, tools, skills, sessions, sandboxes, storage, the agent loop itself all sit behind Cordis plugin boundaries, so you can assemble agent runtimes in configuration without changing source. An append-only session log is the single source of truth (resume/fork/replay share one typed-event stream), and the docs promise compatibility-breaking changes as it iterates. Run it with `npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web` (web UI at 127.0.0.1:3080) or from source at deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness; a Discord community and GitHub Discussions carry feedback. (The deepseek.com/harness page currently returns a "Page moved" placeholder, so this breakdown is corroborated from the public repository and independent coverage rather than the landing page itself.)

title: Delta — multiplayer coding with agents
brief: A multiplayer environment for coding with agents — shared threads where teammates and agents build and review together, with full conversation and code context. Product claims unverified.
warning: Product claims unverified.
details: Delta (delta.dev) — a multiplayer environment for coding with agents (from the Zed folks, per the blog assets). The unit of work is a thread: the conversation with an agent plus the checkout of the repository it works in, kept together as one shareable artifact. Invite teammates into the same thread to review, comment, and work alongside the agent in real time — the thread stays connected to every change so you see the decisions and prompts behind the code, and review feedback stays anchored to lines as the work evolves. Move between desktop, web, or a cloud runner with conversation and code synchronized. Underneath sits DeltaDB, a version-control layer that records work as a stream of fine-grained deltas rather than Git-style commit snapshots — each delta has a stable identity, so a reference anchors to a change instead of a line number and survives as code moves. Thousands of developers reportedly already use Delta as their primary agentic platform; the blog carries pieces on planning in Delta and on agent benchmarks beyond pass rates.

title: Rust Foundation Trusted Training (RFTT)
brief: The Rust Foundation's quality standard for Rust training. Reference material if you're evaluating Rust courses or building one.
details: Rust Foundation Trusted Training (RFTT, rustfoundation.org) — the Rust Foundation's accreditation program: a quality standard recognizing organizations whose Rust training meets its bar for technical accuracy, instructor quality, and learner experience. Accreditation ($3,000/year + $500 one-time application fee, two-year period) requires Rust Foundation membership, 2+ years in business, 1+ year offering Rust training, and review across five areas (credibility/ethics, content quality, instructor competence, transparency/accessibility, evaluation/feedback) by a committee of active training professionals. Five founding providers accredited June 2026: Doulos, Ferrous Systems, Integer 32, Mainmatter, and Wyliodrin. Benefits include the official designation, public listing on rustfoundation.org, referral when organizations ask the Foundation for training, amplification, RustConf perks, and coordinated sales. Note: this accredits organizations and their training, not individual developers — it's not a certification for individuals.

title: Psychology for UX: Study Guide
brief: Nielsen Norman Group's study guide on the psychology behind UX. A solid reference for grounding design decisions in research rather than taste.
details: NNGroup's Psychology for UX study guide — a curated index of their articles and videos on the human psychology that UX design is built on, organized by topic: attention (tunnel vision, change blindness), Gestalt principles (common region, closure, similarity, proximity, figure/ground, continuation, common fate), memory (short-term limits, chunking, cognitive load, peak-end rule, Zeigarnik effect), sensemaking (mental models, information scent/foraging), decision making (prospect theory, choice overload, Hick's law, satisficing), motor processes (Fitts's law, interaction cost, response-time limits), motivation (self-determination theory, fresh-start effect), cognitive biases (halo effect, confirmation bias, anchoring, negativity bias), persuasion and influence, emotion and delight, and attitudes toward technology. Each topic links to both articles and videos with one-line descriptions. The framing: you don't need a psychology degree — the best designs are built for people as they really are. A solid self-study syllabus for designers and design engineers.

title: beUI motion components
brief: Copy-paste animated React components from beUI. Drop-in motion without building animation primitives from scratch.
details: beUI's motion components page — free, open-source animated React components built with Motion and Tailwind, copy-paste TypeScript you own and customize. A large catalog: tilt cards, spring/magnetic/metallic buttons, expressive CTA buttons, expandable controls, adaptive steppers, marquees, tabs with spring layoutId indicators, vaul-inspired bottom sheets, pull-to-refresh, gooey popovers, morphing modals, text/number animations (shimmer, scramble, rolling tickers), theme toggles via the View Transition API, virtualized tables smooth at 10k+ rows, shader backgrounds, cylinder carousels, iOS-style wheel pickers, and loaders with seventeen variants. Composable primitives (sortable lists, image viewers, date pickers, selects, comboboxes) with keyboard navigation, controlled/uncontrolled state, and reduced-motion safety throughout. New additions highlighted at top. For teams that want crafted motion without a dependency — paste it in and tune it.

title: Canvas UI
brief: A creative component library for Canvas, WebGL and WebGPU. For interfaces that need GPU-level visuals rather than DOM elements.
details: Canvas UI (canvasui.dev) is an open-source library of tasteful html-in-canvas components in WebGL or WebGPU — framework-agnostic, with every effect shipping in six flavors (React, Solid, Preact, Vue, Svelte, dependency-free vanilla TypeScript) with the same engine and props. Effects like Blaze, Liquid, Laser, Clouds, Bubble, Droplets, Glass, Magnify, Grid, and Ripple render on the GPU outside React's render cycle, pause off-screen, clean up on unmount, and respect reduced-motion. It's built for agents too: the registry speaks the shadcn protocol, so any assistant with the shadcn MCP server can browse, read docs, and install components from one prompt. License is MIT + Commons Clause — free forever in any app, with resale/redistribution of the components themselves prohibited. Graceful degradation: where the experimental html-on-canvas capability isn't available, content renders as regular HTML and GPU effects run as overlays.

title: treg
brief: A tool catalog for agents — 2,630 endpoints across 47 providers (SEO, social, enrichment, ads data) callable with one key, priced per call, plus support for your own keys and skills. Tom's 2 Sep share carried his referral param; normalized to the root domain.
details: treg.to — "OpenRouter for agent tools and data, pay per call." One unified key across 108 providers and 3,800+ endpoints: your agent holds a single treg token and every tool in the catalog answers to it, with credentials injected server-side (never on a machine). The model: your agent asks for the task, not the tool — treg shows what each provider charges and what they've measured it doing (success rate, speed, last answered), so the agent picks on evidence. No subscription: seats you'd never buy for one agent run (Semrush, Moz, Crunchbase, Hunter) become fractions of a cent per call, price quoted up front, $1 free to start; bring your own key and those calls route unmetered. Zero additional markup — they earn on vendor volume pricing. 100% open source, AGPL. Aimed at giving agents metered access to the data-tool economy without key sprawl.

details: Paper (paper.design) — "the connected canvas for teams shipping with agents": a design platform that connects teams, agents, code, and data on a single HTML/CSS-based design space, so design exports as code with nothing lost in translation. The pitch is the continuous loop: agents sync design tokens, styles, and components between codebase and canvas (one source of truth), pull real content and data from any app/CMS/database instead of lorem ipsum, and handle boilerplate (responsive variants, consistency checks) while humans keep the creative calls. title: Paseo

details: Paseo (getpaseo/paseo, 19.4k stars) — "orchestrate multiple coding agents from desktop and mobile": one interface for Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, OpenCode, Pi, Antigravity, and Muse Code agents. Architecture: a local self-hosted daemon manages your agents on your own machines with your full dev environment; clients span desktop, iOS, Android, web, and CLI, with an end-to-end encrypted relay for phone pairing. Run agents in parallel, pick the right model per job, dictate tasks in voice mode, script everything from the CLI (`paseo run --provider claude/opus-4.6 "..."`), or build on the TypeScript SDK. Skills (`/paseo-handoff`, `/paseo-advisor`, `/paseo-committee`) teach your agent to orchestrate other agents — plan with Claude, hand off to Codex. Privacy-first: no telemetry, tracking, or forced logins. Plugins extend it with themes, panels, and providers. Built by one person, community-funded. Apache-2.0.

title: elxr

An experimental research codebase (from the CheapInfra community's own asx8678) exploring how to make agents reliable over long horizons: governing boundaries are WorkCell (correctness), Context Epoch (prompt efficiency), and an append-only typed event log (truth). The current vertical slice implements canonical event hashing, parent-linked storage, typed semantic turn commits, bounded certified child handoffs, deterministic reducers, verified snapshots, fixed-section 32KiB checkpoints, integrity-bound recall, and OpenAI/Anthropic cache plans — plus a fail-closed checked-code sidecar prototype and a measurable long-horizon research loop (`./autoresearch.sh`). Very much infrastructure research, not a product. Apache-2.0.

title: Fresh
brief: An open-source terminal IDE with zero configuration that brings VS Code-style UX — familiar keybindings, full mouse support, command palette — to the shell. It packs IDE-level features including LSP, multi-cursor editing, magit-style git review with per-hunk staging, TypeScript plugins, multi-GB file handling, and SSH remote editing, plus an orchestrator that runs coding agents (claude, codex, opencode, aider) across worktrees.
details: Fresh (getfresh.dev) — "the terminal IDE, refined": a Rust-built terminal IDE that behaves like a modern GUI editor — Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+C copies, full mouse support, menus, command palette, multi-cursor, no modes to learn (vim mode optional). The standout is the Orchestrator: every task gets its own git worktree with its own tabs, terminals, and agent — hop between tasks with an arrow key while the rest keep working. Each workspace can run any terminal coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or your own command), agents that can resume pick up after restarts, and an agent-facing CLI (`fresh --cmd`, `fresh --skill`) lets agents organize workspaces, start sessions, and drive the editor. Also: hunk-level git review dock, side-by-side diffs, multi-GB files without blocking, SSH/Kubernetes/dev-container remotes, multi-LSP per language, detachable daemon with hot exit, TypeScript plugins in a sandbox, and one static binary installable via curl/Homebrew/winget/AUR/npm. title: Markdown Graphs
brief: Monospace charts and tables for MDX and React. Handy for rendering data visuals that stay crisp in markdown contexts.
details: mdxcn (mdx-graphs.kshv.me) — "markdown-friendly components": a free, open-source set of callouts, steps, terminals, charts, and timelines for MDX, installed via the shadcn CLI. The agent angle: install the skill and your agent can choose a graph, fill in real props, and place it beside the prose — writing JSX for MDX, `::graph-*` for comark, or a knap filter, and in plain Markdown pasting the official ASCII instead of inventing an unreusable diagram. The idea is giving your agent the same component library you have, so generated docs come with real charts rather than ASCII approximations. Browse every component in the library section; the FAQ covers what you install, where it works, and how agents use it.

title: Eclipse Theia
brief: Eclipse Theia — a cloud and desktop IDE framework implemented in TypeScript. The open foundation behind several well-known IDE products.
details: Eclipse Theia (eclipse-theia/theia, 21.7k stars) — a cloud and desktop IDE framework in TypeScript for building full-fledged multi-language IDEs and tools with web technologies. The framework behind many custom IDEs: highly flexible architecture, VS Code extension protocol support, browser-based or Electron desktop targets, under vendor-neutral Eclipse Foundation governance. The repo is the platform source; adopters build their own IDE products on it (examples, extension mechanisms, and VS Code-extension compatibility reports in the docs). Every release now ships an SBOM to the Eclipse Foundation registry. EPL-2.0 (with GPL-2.0-with-classpath-exception as secondary license).

title: Plane
brief: Open-source alternative to Jira, Linear, Monday and ClickUp. A self-hostable project-management option for teams avoiding SaaS lock-in.
details: Plane (makeplane/plane, 60.3k stars) — the heavyweight open-source Jira/Linear/Monday/ClickUp alternative for modern project management: work items with a rich-text editor, cycles (sprints) with burn-down charts, modules for breaking down complex projects, customizable filtered views, Pages (docs with AI), and real-time analytics. Install options: Plane Cloud (fastest), or self-host via Docker/Kubernetes with full control of your data — instance admins get a "God mode" for configuration. Built with React Router, Django, and Node. Active community (forum + GitHub Discussions), 64 releases. AGPL-3.0 — fine for self-hosting, but the copyleft matters if you modify and offer it as a service.

title: Hy4-preview-FP8
brief: Tencent's Hy4 preview weights in FP8 on Hugging Face — 770B total, 49B active, 1M context, open weights. For anyone with the hardware to run a frontier-scale open model.
details: Hy4 preview-FP8 (tencent) — the FP8-quantized open-weights release of Tencent's new Hy4 preview flagship MoE: 770B total parameters, 49B activated per token, 78 layers (256 routed experts + 1 shared per MoE layer, top-8 routed), 1M context, plus a built-in 10B MTP layer for speculative decoding. Architecture borrows from DeepSeek/GLM: gated sparse attention with cross-layer index reuse, identity hyper-connections on the residual path. Tencent positions it at the open-source frontier — blind side-by-side evals by 163 internal experts on 203 engineering tasks had it slightly ahead of GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3. Training data was co-built with in-house software, game, finance, and security experts, and the model is co-designed with Tencent's CodeBuddy/WorkBuddy products. Deploy via vLLM or SGLang (official prebuilt images, OpenAI-compatible API); finetuning pipeline and the AngelSlim compression toolkit included. Apache-2.0. The card is candid about known issues: it can over-reason and over-verify.

title: GLM-5.3-Flash-DFlash2
brief: A GLM-5.3-Flash quant on Hugging Face. Context is thin — thelaggingway's whole review was "Huh" — but it's another fast-model option to know about.
details: GLM-5.3-Flash-DFlash2 (incoai) — not a standalone model but the DFlash 2 draft model for z-ai's GLM-5.3-Flash, used inside a speculative-decoding server. DFlash 2 is a block-diffusion drafter: it predicts a whole block of tokens in a single pass, keeps the top candidates at every position, and a lightweight selector traces one coherent path through them; two-tap dynamic convolutions keep the draft from decaying toward the end of the block. Decoding is lossless — greedy output matches the target model exactly, sampling preserves its distribution. Serve with SGLang (`--speculative-algorithm DFLASH`). Benchmark numbers for this checkpoint were still being re-measured at card time. License is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 for research/evaluation only — contact Inco AI for commercial use. title: ArgusAgent
brief: Microsoft's ArgusAgent — a persistent, reviewed multi-agent runtime for long-horizon research and engineering. Directly relevant to anyone running agents on long tasks.
details: ArgusAgent (microsoft/ArgusAgent, 135 stars) is a persistent, reviewed multi-agent runtime for long-horizon research and engineering — agent work that can plan, execute, verify, pause, and continue beyond a single model turn. Its core idea is the Driver-Harness split: the Driver's seat (what to do next, whether the last result was any good, when to stop) is divided across four roles that may not do each other's jobs — Manager (stage transitions), Planner (next task + required evidence), Engineer (implementation), and Reviewer (read-only verdict). Because the worker can't grade its own work, nobody has to watch it: across 27 campaigns and 1,548 hours it needed a human research decision about once every 310 hours at 95–99% duty cycle. Improvements compound without retraining via scoped Skills and source-linked Wiki findings, and new domains ship as verticals (24 included). Native backends span Copilot CLI, Pi, Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build, Qoder, and DeepSeek; interfaces include a Windows desktop app, terminal cockpit, web UI, and phone. Credentials, payment, irreversible actions, and publication always stop for a human. Technical report on arXiv (2608.05144). MIT.

details: pi-warden (DevMortimer, 157 stars) — guardrails for the Pi coding agent that steer instead of interrupt. It enforces your project rules on every write (a `pi-warden.md` rule like "a bare TODO without a ticket reference is a violation", judged in ~250ms by TypeSafe's Jev decision model), holds only hard-to-undo actions before they run (force push, `reset --hard`, `rm -rf`, DROP — measured at 3 holds per 1,000 calls on real sessions), and crucially tells the agent what it got wrong so the agent fixes it without you: unverified "done" claims get sent back to run the tests (76% of fake "done"s became real test runs in the maintainer's 1,168-session field report), repeated failing fixes trigger a request for a new hypothesis, and huge tool outputs get trimmed to what matters. Everything is calibrated on recorded sessions with published eval reports — rules broken went from 6/150 runs to 0/150 with warden on; features that didn't earn their cost (working-memory pruning, stale-result stubs) didn't ship. Install via `pi install npm:pi-warden`, then `/warden enable` and `/warden init`; the offline guards work without a key. MIT.

details: pi-typesafe (DevMortimer) puts TypeSafe's Jev judgment model inside the Pi coding agent. Jev answers typed questions — choice (which option fits, with probabilities), score (position on an ordered rubric), noul (probability a statement is true) — in well under a second for a fraction of a cent, returning calibrated numbers instead of prose. The package gives Pi three things: the `typesafe_evaluate` agent tool (opt-in per session via `/typesafe enable`) for batched structured judgments like triaging issue lists or scoring candidates against a rubric, a terminal playground (`/typesafe test`, `/typesafe playground`) that runs requests without touching model context, and a typed API so other extensions (like pi-warden) share one client, one key store, and one login prompt instead of each asking for a key. Spending is fenced with per-session attempt caps, daily request/token/USD caps that survive restarts, and a usage ledger; backends beyond TypeSafe itself include OpenRouter, CommandCode, and Liquid AI (whose free d1 model is slow enough to need longer timeouts). title: MiniCPM5-2B-PCD

details: An experimental inference package (monotykamary) applying Parallel Constrained Decoding (PCD) to the unchanged openbmb/MiniCPM5-2B weights — no training, RL, LoRA, or weight modification — for fast finite-choice classification and structured extraction on a 2B model. Token mode branches one question per field and projects the LM head only onto allowed token rows; sequence mode scores complete serialized candidates by normalized log-likelihood. Measured on one L40S in FP32: token PCD averaged 85.61ms versus 694.99ms for autoregressive JSON (8.1x faster), with 88.9% field accuracy versus 94.4% — and 100% schema-valid objects in both. details: LFM2.5-2.6B-RLCD (monotykamary) — an experimental inference-only package implementing Parallel Constrained Decoding (PCD) on unchanged LiquidAI/LFM2.5-2.6B weights. Instead of generating JSON tokens autoregressively, it prefills shared context once, forks the model's attention and convolution state per field, evaluates all allowed answers in parallel (projecting the output head only onto the relevant option-token rows), and serializes a typed JSON object in Python. Two modes: `token` (fast classifier-style per-field decisions, ~9.9x faster than AR JSON on 12 dev cases and 45.6x on a 28-field synthetic case on a single L40S) and `sequence` (full-sequence log-likelihood scoring reference). The card is unusually honest about limits: only 72.2% accuracy on six fresh audit cases vs 94.4% for autoregressive JSON, failed both high-cardinality probes, and the production accuracy gate was not met — returned probabilities are uncalibrated. Weights unchanged from upstream (LFM Open License v1.0, commercial revenue conditions); the PCD inference code is MIT. Includes Modal scripts, benchmarks with raw JSON evidence, and pytest coverage of cache/scoring equivalence. The `RLCD` name follows community naming, not TypeSafe/Jev's actual RL training.

details: Qwen-2.5-1B-RLCD (harshatheg) — a high-throughput Parallel Constrained Decoding inference engine for structured extraction, decision routing, and categorical classification, tuned for Apple Silicon via MLX (benchmarked with mlx-community/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct-4bit on an M4 Max, where it claims 5.6x-7.0x latency reductions over standard autoregressive decoding with 100% schema validity). The trick: single broadcast prefill of the context and schema into one KV cache, broadcast across all schema fields in parallel, sub-vocabulary logit slicing so only valid candidate token IDs are scored, calibrated softmax over the candidate slice, token-tree disambiguation for multi-token enum prefixes, and programmatic JSON assembly — no JSON parsing errors, ever. Includes a developer SDK (`StructuredSchema`/`FieldDefinition` for enums up to 255 choices and booleans), per-field confidence telemetry, a command-line benchmark runner with enterprise presets (fraud routing, code security audit, support triage, tariff classification), an interactive web visualizer comparing PCD vs autoregressive with hallucination detection, and a FastAPI server. details: Varve (monotykamary) is an experimental local-first, tiered time-series database in Rust — "time settles into layers." The design makes data aging a first-class concern without inheriting a full PostgreSQL server: Rust owns the write path, partitions, durability, and policy; Arrow/Parquet owns the columnar representation; DuckDB (v2 alpha) owns SQL execution. Data path: validated measurements → local WAL with fsync → hot rows and incremental rollups → sorted ZSTD Parquet segments → async publication to an S3-compatible object store. Features include append-only numeric time-series tables, stable hash shards with event-time windows, continuous count/sum/min/max/avg and OHLC rollups with retained-raw backfill, lifecycle jobs (flush, compaction, archive/eviction, expiration, GC), and Rust + TypeScript clients plus a JSON CLI, HTTP/WebSocket service, and opt-in PostgreSQL-wire compatibility. A headless CLI inspects node trees, queries with XPath, lints design files, extracts design tokens, scripts via the Figma Plugin API, and exports to PNG/SVG/PDF/PPTX/JSX/Storybook. title: Herdr 0.9 — Connecting the machines
brief: The Herdr blog on 0.9, which brings local and remote machines into one TUI client, with Herdr Cloud coming next. Herdr's pitch: run agents anywhere, leave them running.
details: The Herdr 0.9 blog post "Connecting the machines" — the substance behind the fleet-management announcement. Herdr (a terminal UI for managing coding agents, 700k+ downloads, ~1,000 plugins) previously had one client attached to one server; agents that run for hours want a machine that stays alive 24/7, but each remote machine needed its own client in another terminal tab. In 0.9 the outer UI moved to the client while servers keep owning their sessions and terminal views, so `herdr machine add workbox` brings a remote machine's workspaces, tabs, and agents into the same TUI over SSH — agents keep running when you disconnect. The post is honest about why it took months: multiplexers like tmux/Zellij don't support one TUI managing independent servers, and aggregating sessions meant restructuring where the UI lives. Next: Herdr Cloud as the zero-config middleman (end-to-end encrypted), then cross-machine agent collaboration and session migration as the road to 1.0.

Checking results: read what it needs from you first, ask it to review diffs/PRs before a human does (early testers found it caught more bugs at lowest effort than Opus 5 at high effort), and ask it to mark anything it couldn't confirm. In Claude apps: attach charts and screenshots directly instead of retyping numbers, hand it long decks to check for self-contradictions, and ask for finished files rather than outlines. Also covers the new safeguards — Opus 5.5 is the first Opus with Fable-level bio/cyber guardrails, so flagged messages switch to an older model (disable in Settings if you want to be asked first) — and the /fast research-preview mode for back-and-forth work.

details: BendSR (k3ybladewielder) is a native symbolic-regression implementation built with Bend, Higher Order Company's massively parallel functional language. An evolutionary algorithm breeds expression ASTs concurrently across GPUs/CPUs, and Bend 2's integrated proof checker (LAWS.bend/PROOF.bend) enforces safety invariants — determinism, immutability, numerical safety — during stochastic mutation and crossover, so no division-by-zero or silent NaNs. The cases directory is the fun part: recovering Feynman physics laws, multivariable surfaces, embedded closed-loop control laws for edge devices, interpretable quantitative-finance alpha factors, dynamic-pricing demand curves, GDPR-compliant churn risk scoring, and supply-chain reorder formulas. Runs with `bend src/Main.bend` (CPU) or `bend -c` (GPU); published on Bend Hub as a content-addressed package you can import into your own Bend project. A dataset-loader script converts your CSV/XLSX/Parquet into Bend AST structures. Beyond the algorithm, it is an interesting case study of Bend doing real work plus formal verification of ML-flavored code. MIT.

details: Cloudflare's open-source coding-agent skill (23.9k stars) that turns your agent into a security auditor — and the seed of Cloudflare's own vulnerability-discovery harness. It orchestrates a six-phase audit: reconnaissance (architecture, trust boundaries, and input surfaces into architecture.md plus a deterministic coverage-ledger.json), coverage-led hunting with isolated hunters and coverage critics, adversarial candidate validation where a fresh verifier tries to disprove every finding, structured output to findings.json with `confirmed`/`needs_validation`/`rejected` verdicts validated against a schema, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting (REPORT.md, FINDINGS-DETAIL.md, NEEDS-VALIDATION.md). Attack-class playbooks cover memory safety and binary/kernel targets, LLM prompt injection, web protocol and auth, client-side/DOM, supply chain and CI/release, cloud and IAM, RPC and messaging, resource exhaustion, data isolation, and desktop/mobile IPC. Design principles: only confirm established boundary failures, adversarial validation (the checker is never the finder), severity requires demonstrated impact, defense-in-depth gaps are hardening notes not vulnerabilities, and multiple runs improve coverage. Install with `npx skills add`; needs a tool-using agent with parallel subagents, Node.js, and an OS-enforced sandbox. MIT.

title: Saving 100TB of RAM with math
brief: Cloudflare engineering deep-dive on saving 100TB of RAM with math (and Rust). A solid systems-engineering read.
details: A Cloudflare engineering blog post on how small changes to the consistent-hashing algorithm in the Pingora Backend Router reclaimed over 100TB of RAM globally — on top of 100TB the DNS team shed earlier. The root cause: PBR needed dozens of separate consistent-hash rings (one per feature combination), each holding many hashes per server, ballooning to 6GB of hash structures in some cases. Two fixes: a struct-layout insight (the 32-bit server index was wasteful since PBR will never coordinate 65k+ servers; shrinking to a raw `[u8; 6]` byte array with getters dodged Rust's alignment padding and cut memory 25%), and exact math for the error margin per hash count, showing the last 90,000 hashes bought a minuscule 0.7% reduction — so fewer hashes suffice. The post is also a genuinely good explainer: day-one probability (expected value, standard deviation, coefficient of variation), why 160 hashes per server is the NGINX default, how ketama weighting scales by disk space, and why `#[repr(packed)]` was passed over. Worth reading for any systems engineer — a masterclass in how layout awareness plus a little math saves hardware at scale.

title: Bend
brief: Bend 2 — a fast programming language that blocks AI mistakes via proof checking. Install with curl from bend-lang.com.
details: Bend 2 (bendlang/bend, 23.3k stars, by Victor Taelin's team) — "a fast language that blocks AI mistakes via proof." The pitch is threefold: it runs as fast as C on the CPU and CUDA on the GPU (the entire language runs on the GPU with full memory unification), it checks mathematical proofs orders of magnitude faster than Isabelle/Agda/Lean/Rocq (sub-second checks that take other provers minutes), and it is parallel by default — no threads, no locks, no kernels; split work in two and it spreads across every core. The signature feature is LAWS.bend: declare rules your app must never break ("the sum of all balances must be zero", "players can never pass through solid walls", "winning is impossible"), and the compiler mechanically demands a correctness proof whenever code is edited, making violations impossible — their demo shows an AI merging a wrap-around bug without laws, and being forced to fix it with them. Syntax reads like Python with dependent types. Get started with `curl -fsSL https://bend-lang.com/install.sh | sh`, then tell your agent to `bend guide`, keep important rules in LAWS.bend, and run `bend PROOF.bend` before committing. The limitations list is refreshingly honest: Bend 2 is young (Bend 1 programs don't carry over), annotations are verbose, no Windows, no TLS/HTTP/JSON/regex yet, the compiler is 99% AI-written and not fully audited, and the JS target is single-core. Apache-2.0.

brief: Shared by thelaggingway with just "Another one" — context is thin, but it landed in the search-tool thread. Worth a look if you're tracking search APIs.
details: Jev Search (superagents-lab, 507 stars) — search the web in plain language, with a decision model doing the query understanding. Type the request as you would say it ("Rust async runtimes on Hacker News this month"), and a decision model such as TypeSafe's Jev or Cloudflare's Clef chooses the sources, time range, and search terms, then ranks results returned through Search1API. You get links and snippets with visible relevance scores and editable filters — no generated answers. Under the hood: Google, DuckDuckGo, and Yandex for open web; Hacker News, Reddit, and GitHub combine site-restricted Google with dedicated engines; X, arXiv, YouTube, Wikipedia, IMDb, and WeChat use vertical engines — all called concurrently and streamed as newline-delimited JSON. Deployable to Cloudflare Workers (TanStack Start, React, KV cache, rate limits), installable as a PWA, with a model selector (Jev, Clef, Clef-flash) and fallback provider chains. Built by Search1API as an independent project, not an official TypeSafe product. MIT.
